opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've been thinking about for a while. The original inspiration is pretty simple. When you go buy a fridge or a washing machine, you don't need to understand compressors or motor efficiency. You look at the sticker, and it tells you roughly how this one compares to the others on the shelf. With AI right now we have nothing like that. People choose models based on leaderboards that only measure accuracy or some benchmark score, and energy is completely invisible.

So the idea is to give people that missing dimension. You take a set of standardized tasks, things like text generation, summarization, image generation, classification, and you run models on the same hardware under the same conditions. You measure how much energy they use for a fixed amount of work, and then you bucket them, say one to five stars, relative to other models doing that same task. The comparison has to be within a task. It doesn't make sense to compare an image generator to a sentiment classifier.

For it to become an official standard, a few things need to happen. First, the methodology has to be open and reproducible, so anyone can verify a score and it isn't just a company grading its own homework. Second, it has to be updated regularly, because the field moves so fast that what counts as five stars today might be middle of the pack in six months. Third, and this is the hard part, you need buy-in, ideally from a neutral body. That could be a standards organization or a government agency, the way the EPA runs the actual Energy Star program, or some kind of multi-stakeholder consortium.

The real challenge is closed models. With open-weight models we can run them ourselves and measure. With models that sit behind an API, we can't see the hardware, the batching, or anything else, so we have to rely on the companies disclosing that information. That's why I think regulation has a role here. Voluntary disclosure has mostly not worked. Companies have become less transparent about energy and emissions over the last few years, not more.

What I'd really like to see is the rating become part of procurement. If governments, universities, and big companies say "we'll take energy efficiency into account when we choose an AI provider," that creates a market incentive, and suddenly developers care about efficiency, not just about topping the leaderboard. And for regular users, I hope it helps people realize that you don't always need the biggest generative model. Sometimes a small, task-specific model does the job just as well and uses a tiny fraction of the energy. A label helps make that choice visible.

r001.rationale: The response mentions the EPA as an example of a neutral body, but does not identify its focus on tangible physical objects as a barrier to rating AI models.

r002.rationale: The response suggests a standards organization, government agency, or multi-stakeholder consortium, but does not propose partnering with ISO or NIST.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've been working on for a few years now, and the analogy to Energy Star is really deliberate. When you go buy a refrigerator or a washing machine, you don't have to be an electrical engineer to make a reasonable decision about efficiency. There's a label, there's a scale, and you can compare across products in a way that's standardized. And right now with AI models, we have nothing like that. You have companies releasing models with basically zero information about how much energy went into training them, let alone what it costs to run them at inference time, which is actually where most of the energy goes once a model is deployed at scale.

So what we did with the AI Energy Score project at Hugging Face was essentially build a first version of that. We take models, we run them on a fixed set of tasks, text generation, image generation, summarization, and so on, on standardized hardware, and we measure the energy consumed per task. And then we give them a rating, one to five stars, relative to other models in that same category. The important thing is that it's task-specific, because a model that's efficient for classification might be terrible for image generation, and comparing across those makes no sense.

Now, in terms of making it an official standard, I think there are a few things that need to happen. The first is that the measurement methodology has to be agreed upon by more than just us. We've tried to be very transparent about how we do it, but ideally you'd have something like a standards body, whether that's ISO or IEEE or even a regulatory agency, saying this is the protocol, this is how you measure, these are the hardware configurations that count. Because otherwise you get companies self-reporting using whatever methodology makes them look best, and that's actually worse than nothing because it creates a false sense of comparability.

The second piece is that the closed model providers have to participate. Right now we can test open models because we can run them ourselves. For the proprietary APIs, we're essentially dependent on the companies either giving us access or disclosing numbers, and most of them don't. So I'd love to see something where, if you're going to deploy a model at a certain scale, or sell access to it, there's a disclosure requirement, and that's where policy comes in. The EU AI Act actually has some language about energy reporting for general-purpose models, and I think that's a really promising lever, even if the details are still being worked out.

And then the third thing, honestly, is adoption on the demand side. Energy Star worked partly because governments made procurement decisions based on it. If large organizations, public institutions, cloud providers, started saying we'll only deploy models that have been rated, or we'll preferentially choose more efficient ones, that creates the market pressure. Because right now, there's no incentive. Efficiency isn't a competitive advantage in the way that benchmark scores are, and I'd like to change that.

So I don't think it's a crazy ask. We've done this for appliances, for cars, for buildings. The technology to measure it exists. It's really a question of political will and getting the industry to accept that this is part of what responsible deployment means.

r001.rationale: The response does not identify the EPA’s focus on tangible physical objects as a barrier.

r002.rationale: It proposes that a standards body such as ISO establish the measurement protocol, describing a route to institutional adoption.

astra-6.text:
I’d like to see us get to a point where, when you’re choosing an AI model, you can see how much energy it uses alongside how well it performs. An Energy Star-style rating could make that information accessible without expecting everyone to understand the technical details of measuring energy consumption.

To make it an official standard, we’d need a common measurement methodology: what task are we testing, on what hardware, and under what conditions? Otherwise, you’re comparing numbers that don’t necessarily mean the same thing. That would need collaboration between researchers, model developers, and standards bodies, with independent verification.

And I’d want it to help people make choices. If a smaller model meets your needs using much less energy, that should be visible. The goal is to make efficiency something we measure and value alongside accuracy.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the need for a common measurement method but does not identify the EPA’s focus on tangible physical objects as a barrier.

r002.rationale: It calls for collaboration with standards bodies but does not propose partnering with ISO or NIST.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d like to see it become something that’s standardized and independently verified, so that we’re comparing models on the same basis. You’d need a clear methodology for measuring energy use, and transparency about what’s included—whether that’s training a model or running it, for example.

And I don’t think it should just be one number that says a model is good or bad. It should help people understand the trade-offs: for the task you want to do, how much energy does this model use, and is there a smaller, more efficient model that would meet your needs?

Ideally, that information would be available right where people choose a model. Then it becomes something developers can act on, and something procurement policies and eventually regulation can build on.

r001.rationale: The response discusses standardization and measurement but does not identify the EPA’s focus on tangible physical objects as a barrier.

r002.rationale: The response calls for standardization and independent verification but does not propose partnering with ISO or NIST.
